1. Probability Space Probability theory is a branch of mathematics that studies the laws governing random phenomena, i.e. phenomena in which chance intervenes, such as a throw of a dice. In this chapter, we will describe the framework of probability and establish its terminology. We will not separate the presentation of the definitions from the role they play in modelling a concrete situation. A short history of probability 1 Today, probabilities are everywhere: they are at the heart of quantum physics, in the practical prediction of temporal processes (the stock market, the weather), in medical research, and so on. The term “probability” was first used in medieval jurisprudence. It comes from the Latin word “probare”, which means “to predict”. The calculation of probabilities was then an “art” whose aim was to determine the likelihood of an event. The development of probability as a mathematical science is therefore closely linked to games. The first problems were linked to games of dice and cards: the aim was to count the number of possibilities for a certain configuration to appear (e.g. the sum of two dice equals 7). But the problem that really launched the development of probability theory was the famous problem of points. 1 All the historical notes and remarks are mainly taken from the article Calcul des probabilités , Michel Loève, from the book Abrégé d'histoire des mathématiques 1700-1900 , under the direction of Jean Dieudonné, Tome II, Hermann, 1978.

Problem of points n players, each having initially bet a sum of money k , play a game of chance. The game stops when one of the players has won N rounds and the winner takes all the money bet nk . How should the prize be distributed if, for any reason whatsoever, the game is interrupted before the end? Some of the great Italian mathematicians of the 15th and 16th centuries (Pacioli, Cardano, Tartaglia), the same school that found the general solution to cubic equations and introduced complex numbers, tackled this problem but failed to provide a correct answer. The three founding fathers of the theory of probability are: ★ Blaise Pascal, French mathematician, who in 1654, in his correspondence with Pierre de Fermat, found the correct solution to the problem of points. The solution is closely related to Pascal's famous triangle, and uses the concept of probability of victory without actually saying so. ★ Christiaan Huygens, the great Dutch scientist of the 17th century, who in 1657 published De Ratiociniis in Ludo Aleae , the first work in which the concept of probability was rigorously stated and which recognised the importance of probabilities beyond games. 2 ★ Jacob Bernoulli, Swiss mathematician and physicist, who, in his posthumous work Ars Conjectandi of 1713, addresses the problem of a game of chance with two outcomes (win/loss) that is repeated identically n times (the famous Bernoulli experiment ). This was followed by a period of two hundred years with some important advances made mainly by the school of French mathematicians at the École Polytechnique (Poisson, Laplace) and the Russian school in Saint Petersburg (Chebychev, Markov, Lyapunov) (see pages 76 and 115 for details). That said, until the 1930s, probability theory remained, for mathematicians, a small part of applied mathematics with little theoretical interest. The situation changed radically with the work of the Russian mathematician Andreï Kolmogorov who, in his 1933 book Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung , rigorously formalised the whole theory of probability by linking it to measure theory, a branch of mathematics developed by Henri-Léon Lebesgue (see section 1.4). 3 Portrait of Paul Pierre Levy, an elderly man with glasses and a mustache, wearing a suit and tie. 1.1 Basic concepts Definition 1.1 (Random experiment, Sample space) A random experiment is a procedure whose outcome cannot be determined with certainty. The set of all possible outcomes is called the sample space , usually denoted by \Omega . Remark: By convention, all sample spaces are non empty, since we suppose that the random experiment under consideration has at least one possible outcome. Examples: i) When throwing a coin, \Omega = \{H, T\} where H means Heads and T means Tails. ii) When throwing a six-faced dice, the sample space is simply \Omega = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\} . The outcome of a throw is represented by the number of the face facing upwards. iii) When throwing two six-faced dice, the sample space is \Omega = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}^2 . The outcome of this experiment is represented by the number shown in the first dice and the number shown in the second dice. iv) When measuring the lifetime of a smartphone (in days), one can decide to take \Omega = \mathbb{N} as the sample space. v) If we are at the bus stop and we know that the bus comes exactly every twelve minutes but we do not know when did the last bus come, our waiting time can be seen as a random experiment whose sample space is \Omega = [0, 12] . Definition 1.2 (Events) Given a random experiment, we call: ★ event , any subset of the sample space \Omega , ★ certain event , the event \Omega , ★ impossible event , the event \emptyset . Remark: This innocent-looking definition of events is problematic in the case of uncountable sample spaces, such as the one from the last example (the curious student can read section 1.4 to understand the subtleties of uncountable sample spaces). In this course, unless otherwise stated, we will always consider finite or countable sample spaces

Examples: In the previous examples, we can consider: i) The event E = \text{“Heads”} = \{H\} . ii) The event E = \text{“the outcome is an even number”} . iii) The event E = \text{“the sum of both dice is 7”} . iv) The event E = \text{“the lifetime of the smartphone exceeds three years”} . v) The event E = \text{“to wait less than five minutes”} . 1.2 Review of set theory Definition 1.3 (Basic set operations) Let \Omega be any set. Then: 1. Subset. E is a subset of \Omega , denoted E \subset \Omega , if \forall x \in E, x \in \Omega . E is called a proper subset if E \subset \Omega , E \neq \Omega and E \neq \emptyset . 2. Complement. Given a subset E of \Omega , the complement of E in \Omega is the set \bar{E} = \{x \in \Omega \mid x \notin E\} . 3. Union. Given two subsets E and F of \Omega , their union is the set E \cup F = \{x \in \Omega \mid (x \in E) \text{ or } (x \in F)\}. 4. Intersection. Given two subsets E and F of \Omega , their intersection is the set E \cap F = \{x \in \Omega \mid (x \in E) \text{ and } (x \in F)\} . These four operations can be seen from a logical point of view as logical connectives, but they can also be seen as describing occurrences of events of random experiments: Logical connectives Operations on sets Occurrence of events AND Intersection E \cap F the two events occur OR Union E \cup F at least one event occurs NOT Complement \bar{E} E does not occur \implies Subset E \subset F Each time that E occurs also F occurs Proposition 1.1 : Algebraic structure of set operations The basic operations on sets satisfy the following properties: 1. Commutativity of \cup and \cap : \forall (E, F) \subset \Omega^2, E \cup F = F \cup E \text{ and } E \cap F = F \cap E. 2. Associativity of \cup and \cap : \forall (E, F, G) \subset \Omega^3, (E \cup F) \cup G = E \cup (F \cup G) \text{ and } (E \cap F) \cap G = E \cap (F \cap G). 3. Idempotence of \cup and \cap : \forall E \subset \Omega, E \cup E = E = E \cap E. 4. \emptyset is the identity element of \cup and \Omega is the identity element of \cap : \forall E \subset \Omega, E \cup \emptyset = E = E \cap \Omega. 5. \Omega is the absorbing element of \cup and \emptyset is the absorbing element of \cap : \forall E \subset \Omega, E \cup \Omega = \Omega \text{ and } E \cap \emptyset = \emptyset. 6. Distributivity of \cup over \cap and of \cap over \cup : \forall (E, F, G) \subset \Omega^3, (E \cup F) \cap G = (E \cap G) \cup (F \cap G) \text{ and } (E \cap F) \cup G = (E \cup G) \cap (F \cup G).

Figure 1.5 – Two incompatible events. Definition 1.5 (Partition) Let \mathcal{A} = \{A_1, \dots, A_n\} be a family of possible events of \Omega . We say that \mathcal{A} is a partition of \Omega if the events satisfy the following two properties: 1. \bigcup_{1 \leq i \leq n} A_i = \Omega (the events cover all possible outcomes), 2. \forall 1 \leq i, j \leq n, i \neq j \implies A_i \cap A_j = \emptyset (the events are mutually incompatible). Examples: i) In the random experiment “randomly pick a card in a 52-card deck”, the following events form a partition: A_1 = \text{“the card is a figure or an Ace”}, A_2 = \text{“the card is a number between 7 and 10”}, A_3 = \text{“the card is a number between 2 and 6”}. ii) In the random experiment “randomly pick a word in the dictionary”, the following events form a partition: A_1 = \text{“the word starts with a vowel”}, A_2 = \text{“the word starts with a consonant and appears before the word elephant”}, A_3 = \text{“the word starts with a consonant and appears after the word excellent”}. iii) In the random experiment “randomly pick a student from EFREI”, the following events form a partition: A_1 = \text{“the student is part of the programmes experts”}, A_2 = \text{“the student is in the cycle licence du programme grande école”}, A_3 = \text{“the student is in alternance in the masters cycle du programme grande école”}, A_4 = \text{“the student is in the masters cycle du programme grande école without alternance”}. 1.3 Probability functions We now try to assign to each of these events a number that represents the degree of confidence we have in its occurrence. We call this number the probability of the event. This is a real number with the interpretation that the greater the probability, the greater our confidence in the occurrence of the event. Intuitively, we identify the probability of an event with the asymptotic frequency with which that event occurs when the experiment is repeated infinitely often. So, by repeating an experiment N times, under the same conditions, and noting f_N(A) the frequency with which event A occurs, we take: P(A) = \lim_{N \rightarrow \infty} f_N(A) But this frequentist approach to probabilities has many problems, namely: ★ how do we know that the sequence f_N(A) converges? And if it does, how do we know that it always converges to the same limit? ★ how do we interpret probabilities for random experiments that cannot be renewed?

For these reasons, the modern mathematical approach is to give an abstract axiomatic definition that is neutral from any interpretation, while still checking that these axioms are compatible with our intuitions on what probabilities mean. Definition 1.6 (Probability function) Let \Omega be a finite or countable set. Denote by \mathcal{P}(\Omega) the power set of \Omega (the set of all subsets). A probability function over \Omega is a function P : \mathcal{P}(\Omega) \rightarrow \mathbb{R} such that: 1. \forall E \subset \Omega, 0 \leq P(E) \leq 1 . 2. P(\Omega) = 1 . 3. Additivity : for any sequence (A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} of mutually incompatible events, we have P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^n P(A_i) The pair (\Omega, P) is called a probability space , and for any event E \in \mathcal{P}(\Omega) , the number P(E) \in [0, 1] is called the probability of E . ◆ Examples: i) Uniform probability 4 : Let \Omega be a finite set, E \subset \Omega an event and define P : \mathcal{P}(\Omega) \rightarrow \mathbb{R} by P(E) = \frac{\text{card}(E)}{\text{card}(\Omega)} \quad (\text{"favourable outcomes over possible outcomes"}) Then P is a probability function over \Omega , called uniform over \Omega since all elementary events have equal probability. This uniform probability shows up in many situations and, in this case, the computation of probabilities is reduced to a computation of cardinalities. ii) Let \Omega = \{\omega_1, \omega_2, \dots\} be a finite or countable sample space. Then, any function p : \Omega \rightarrow [0, 1] such that \sum_{\Omega} p(\omega_i) = 1 can be used to define a probability function over \Omega through \forall E \in \mathcal{P}(\Omega), P(E) = \sum_{x \in E} p(x). In other words, any probability function is completely determined by a sequence of positive real numbers whose sum equals 1. 4 This example makes the link between the abstract axiomatic approach and the intuition of what probabilities are.

Proposition 1.3 Let (\Omega, P) be a probability space. Then: * P(\emptyset) = 0 , * P(\bar{E}) = 1 - P(E) , * E \subset F \implies P(E) \leq P(F) , * P(E \cup F) = P(E) + P(F) - P(E \cap F) . Proof. First of all, you only need to look again at the drawings of operations on sets and think of probability as the relative surface of a subset to get an intuitive understanding of these results. Formally (this is a good exercise to familiarise yourself with the properties of probability functions) * We have \emptyset \cap \Omega = \emptyset and \emptyset \cup \Omega = \Omega therefore P(\emptyset \cup \Omega) = P(\emptyset) + P(\Omega) = P(\Omega) . This yields P(\emptyset) = 0 . * Since E \cap \bar{E} = \emptyset , we have P(E \cup \bar{E}) = P(E) + P(\bar{E}) . Moreover, we have E \cup \bar{E} = \Omega . This yields P(E) + P(\bar{E}) = P(\Omega) = 1 . * If E \subset F , we have F = E \cup (F \cap \bar{E}) . Moreover, since E \cap (F \cap \bar{E}) = \emptyset , we have P(F) = P(E) + P(F \cap \bar{E}) . Finally, since P(F \cap \bar{E}) \geq 0 , we have P(F) \geq P(E) . * We have E \cup F = E \cup (F \cap \bar{E}) . Since E \cap (F \cap \bar{E}) = \emptyset , we have P(E \cup F) = P(E) + P(F \cap \bar{E}) . Moreover, F = (E \cap F) \cup (F \cap \bar{E}) and these last two events are incompatible. Thus P(F) = P(E \cap F) + P(F \cap \bar{E}) and we conclude that P(E \cup F) = P(E) + P(F) - P(E \cap F) . \square Proposition 1.4 : Inclusion-Exclusion principle (Poincaré's formula) Let (\Omega, P) be a probability space \{E_1, E_2, \dots, E_n\} any family of events. In the face of this problem, the attitude of modern probability theory is to accept that it is not possible to assign a probability to all subsets of the sample space and restrict the class of subsets that are allowed to be called events. In order to clarify the type of subsets that are allowed to be considered as events, Borel and Lebesgue introduced, at the turn of the 19th century, the following definition:
Let \Omega be a set. A \sigma -algebra over \Omega is a family \mathcal{A} of subsets of \Omega such that

1. \mathcal{A} is not empty: \emptyset \in \mathcal{A} , 2. \mathcal{A} is stable under complements: A \in \mathcal{A} \implies \bar{A} \in \mathcal{A} , 3. \mathcal{A} is stable under countable unions: for any sequence (A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} of subsets of \mathcal{A} , \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} A_n is again a member of \mathcal{A} .

★ The power set \mathcal{P}(\Omega) is always a \sigma -algebra. ★ We call Borel \sigma -algebra of the set [0, 1] the smallest \sigma -algebra that contains all intervals [a, b] with a, b \in [0, 1] . The Borel \sigma -algebra is the \sigma -algebra used in most cases when dealing with probabilities in uncountable spaces. In particular, it does not contain the Vitali sets.

We can at last give the precise modern definition that is the starting point of probability theory, given in 1933 by the Russian mathematician Andreï Kolmogorov : Definition 1.9 (Probability space) A probability space is a triplet (\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P) where: ★ the sample space \Omega is any set. ★ the set of events \mathcal{F} is a \sigma -algebra over \Omega . ★ the probability measure P is a map P : \mathcal{F} \rightarrow [0, 1] such that i) P(\Omega) = 1 . ii) for any sequence of mutually incompatible events (A_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{+\infty} A_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^{+\infty} P(A_i).

Exercise 1.2 [***] Symmetric difference Let \Omega be a set. The proposition 1.1 suggests that the structure of (\mathcal{P}(\Omega), \cup, \cap) is that of a ring. Indeed, \cup and \cap would play the roles of + and \times , whereas \Omega and \emptyset would play the roles of 1 and 0. However, there is a crucial difference: in a ring of numbers, any element admits an opposite (we can perform subtractions), whereas elements of \mathcal{P}(\Omega) do not have an opposite: \forall A \in \mathcal{P}(\Omega), A \neq \emptyset, \nexists B \in \mathcal{P}(\Omega), A \cup B = \emptyset . 2. Conditional probabilities In practical computations of probabilities, we are quickly confronted with two types of situation which lead us to introduce the concept of "conditional probability": ★ Firstly, there are situations where we have partial information about the outcome of the random experiment, information that must be taken into account because it often modifies the probabilities of the outcome. The probability that a person is under 20 years of age is not the same if we also know that this person is a student at EFREI or that he or she is capable of proving the central limit theorem. ★ Then, even when partial information is not known, it is often easier to calculate the probability we want by making a distinction between cases: if we want to calculate the probability that a citizen of the European Union will vote for the Green party in the next European elections, the easiest way is to look at what happens country by country (probability knowing that he or she is French, German, Hungarian, etc).

2.1 Definition and basic properties Definition 2.1 (Conditional probability) Let (\Omega, P) be a probability space and let E, F be two events of \Omega such that F is not impossible. Then, the probability of E knowing F (or conditional probability of E on F ), denoted P(E|F) or P_F(E) , is defined by: P_F(E) = P(E|F) = \frac{P(E \cap F)}{P(F)}. This definition should be easy to understand: everything happens as if F had occurred, so we're only looking at the set F which “replaces” the sample space \Omega . Figure 2.1: A diagram illustrating conditional probability. It shows two Venn diagrams. The left diagram shows a sample space Omega (grey rectangle) containing two overlapping circles E and F. The intersection of E and F is shaded blue. The right diagram shows the same sample space Omega, but with a hatched background, indicating that the sample space is now restricted to F. The intersection of E and F is still shaded blue, but the area of E that does not overlap with F is now hatched, indicating it is ignored. An arrow labeled 'Condition on F' points from the left diagram to the right diagram. Figure 2.1 – The probability of occurrence of event E is the ratio of the blue surface over the surface of the whole sample space (grey area). When conditioning on F (right figure), the sample space becomes smaller and the hatched area is ignored. ◆ Example: Consider the following experiment: we draw, successively and without replacement, two balls from an urn that contains initially two black balls and two white balls. Consider the event E “the first draw yields a white ball” and the event F “the second draw yields a white ball”. Clearly, we have P(E) = \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2} . Moreover, the occurrence (or non-occurrence) of E clearly changes the probability of occurrence of F . Indeed, P(F|E) = \frac{1}{3} and P(F|\bar{E}) = \frac{2}{3} . From node E, it branches into two sub-paths: the upper one is labeled P(F|E) = 1/3 and leads to a node labeled F; the lower one is labeled P(F-bar|E) = 2/3 and leads to a node labeled F-bar. From node E-bar, it branches into two sub-paths: the upper one is labeled P(F|E-bar) = 2/3 and leads to a node labeled F; the lower one is labeled P(F-bar|E-bar) = 1/3 and leads to a node labeled F-bar. All nodes are marked with blue dots. The definition of conditional probability gives us the probability that we draw two white balls: P(E \cap F) = P(F|E) \times P(E) = \frac{1}{6} . We “ read the probability of the intersection ” by multiplying the conditional probabilities that appear along the tree . Notice that, at each branching, the sum of all probabilities equals 1. All this information can also be summarised in a contingency table as follows: E \bar{E} F P(F \cap E) = \frac{1}{6} P(F \cap \bar{E}) = \frac{1}{3} \bar{F} P(\bar{F} \cap E) = \frac{1}{3} P(\bar{F} \cap \bar{E}) = \frac{1}{6} Proposition 2.1 Let (\Omega, P) be a probability space, E and F two events of \Omega such that F is not impossible. Then, we have P(E|F) + P(\bar{E}|F) = 1. Proof. This should be an intuitively obvious result. Formally, we have, by definition: P(E|F) + P(\bar{E}|F) = \frac{P(E \cap F) + P(\bar{E} \cap F)}{P(F)}. Now, since the events E \cap F and \bar{E} \cap F are incompatible, we have P(E \cap F) + P(\bar{E} \cap F) = P((E \cap F) \cup (\bar{E} \cap F)) = P((E \cup \bar{E}) \cap F) = P(\Omega \cap F) = P(F). This shows the result. □ The terminology of conditional probability is justified since:

2.2 Bayes' formula The purpose of Bayes' formula is to allow us to go from P(E|A) to P(A|E) . There are many situations where this problem is of great interest. Let us take a simple example from statistics in medicine, where there are enough patients with a certain pathology coming into a department. We receive sick patients and we can easily calculate the proportion who have been vaccinated, for example. So we have two events: sick S and vaccinated V . This count gives us the proportion of vaccinated patients among the incoming patients, i.e. the probability P(V|S) . But what we are interested in is the probability of falling ill knowing that you have been vaccinated, i.e. P(S|V) 1 . Theorem 2.6 : Bayes' theorem Let \mathcal{A} = \{A_1, \dots, A_n\} be a partition of \Omega and E be any event. Then, we have P(A_j|E) = \frac{P(E|A_j)P(A_j)}{\sum_{i=1}^n P(E|A_i)P(A_i)}. Proof. It suffices to combine the total probability formula and the definition of conditional probabilities to obtain Bayes' theorem. Indeed: P(A_j|E) = \frac{P(A_j \cap E)}{P(E)} = \frac{P(E|A_j)P(A_j)}{P(E)} = \frac{P(E|A_j)P(A_j)}{\sum_{i=1}^n P(E|A_i)P(A_i)}. □ Remark: Often, events A_j are thought of as “hypotheses” and in this case Bayes' formula shows us how to modify our opinions about these hypotheses when an event E occurs (see 2.3 for more details on this point of view on probability as a confidence measure). ♦ Example: A doctor is called in to see a sick child. The doctor has prior information that 90% of the sick children in this neighbourhood have influenza, while the remaining 10% have measles. For the sake of simplicity, let's assume that there are no other illnesses in this neighbourhood. A well-known symptom of measles is a rash. Let's assume that the probability of getting a rash if you have measles is 0.95. However, sometimes children with flu also develop a rash, and the probability of having a rash if you have flu is 0.1. On examining the child, the doctor finds a rash. What is the likelihood of the child having measles? On pose les events G = “to have the flu” R = “to have measles” EC = “to develop a rash” We want to compute P(R|EC) . The events G and R constitute a partition and, according to Bayes' theorem, we have: P(R|EC) = \frac{P(EC|R)P(R)}{P(EC|R)P(R) + P(EC|G)P(G)} = \frac{0.95 \times 0.1}{0.95 \times 0.1 + 0.1 \times 0.9} \approx 0.51. So the child has almost as much chance of having measles as flu!

Historical Note #1 (Thomas Bayes and “his” formula) Thomas Bayes (1701-1761) was a British mathematician who was destined for oblivion: his work on probability was published in 1761 after his death and found very few readers. But his formula was rediscovered in 1774 by the brilliant young French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace. It was Laplace who gave it the name "Bayes' Theorem" in 1781 after a visit from Richard Price, a friend of Bayes, who told him about the British mathematician's work. What's more, Laplace placed Bayes' formula at the centre of a new interpretation of probability, known today as Bayesian, even though there is no evidence that Thomas Bayes himself subscribed to this interpretation. 2.3 (Hors programme) : un peu de philosophie Probability is the most important concept in modern science, especially as nobody has the slightest notion what it means Bertrand Russell After the work of Andreï Kolmogorov in the 1930s, a mathematician has no doubts about what a probability is: he will simply take the abstract definition 1.6, page 15 (or more exactly the even more abstract definition 1.9, page 23). But, as soon as we leave the strict confines of mathematics - and it is precisely outside mathematics that probability acquires its importance - the precise meaning of the concept of "probability" is much more elusive than we might naively believe. Statements such as "the probability that I will roll a six on the next throw of the dice is 1/6 " or "the probability that this carbon-14 atom will decay in the next 5734 years is 0.5" are taken as objective descriptions of a certain reality in the world. Here, their interpretation seems clear enough: for example, the first statement says that, if I repeated the throw of the dice 600 times, I would land on 6 approximately one hundred times and that if I made an infinite number of throws, the proportion of times I would land on 6 would be exactly one sixth. This interpretation of probabilities is known as the frequency interpretation: Frequency interpretation of probabilities The probability of event E is understood as the relative frequency of occurrence of event E in a infinitely long run of repetitions of the random experiment. This interpretation was implicit in De Moivre, Poisson and Gauss and was defined explicitly by Mills, Ellis, Cournot and Fries. It was the dominant view in science until the beginning of the twentieth century and continues to be so in common discussion today. But, apart from the obvious problems associated with the appearance of infinity in this definition 2 , the frequency interpretation becomes more problematic for statements like "the probability of rain tomorrow is 80%" or, even worse, "the probability of Carlos Alcaraz winning the next US Open tennis tournament is 30%". The main problem is clearly that the experiments in question cannot be repeated. But an even deeper problem is that we can question the objective nature of the preceding assertions and see them as assertions about the subjective knowledge and beliefs of the person proclaiming them. 2 Take a counter-intuitive probability result, for example the one in exercise 1.13, and try to convince your non-scientific friends who are reluctant to accept the result by experiment. You will see that, very often, the experiment will prove you wrong, to which you will retort, somewhat embarrassed: "If we had repeated the experiment more times, you would have seen that the result is true". To give an easy, concrete example: the probability that, out of 10,000 throws of a coin, there are exactly 5,000 heads and 5,000 tails is only 0.008!

Bayesian or subjective interpretation of probabilities The probability of event E is a measure of the subjective belief that a person has in the future occurrence of event E given her current state of knowledge. According to this view, the claim “the probability that the dice will yield a six in the next throw is 1/6 ” shows, in fact, that one has no knowledge about the precise speed and angular momentum of the dice when it will leave the hand of the person throwing the dice and about the details of how fair the dice is. Therefore, in Bayesianism, probabilities are always conditional probabilities (there is no meaning to what an absolute probability could be) and Bayes’ theorem describes precisely the process of learning: the formula shows how the beliefs (of a rational agent) on information A_j evolve as we discover the existence of certain events E . This second approach to the meaning of probabilities turned out to be very productive in statistics since it motivated a whole branch of the field called Bayesian inference. Exercise 2.22 [***] A sequence of probabilities At a time when each operator had a third of the mobile telecommunications market, three operators A , B and C decided to launch a new type of annual package. At the end of the year, market share changes as follows: ★ The customers of company A split equally between A , B and C the following year. ★ Customers of company B always remain loyal to this company. ★ The customers of the company C will be the following year customers of A with a probability \frac{1}{12} , of B with a probability \frac{7}{12} and of C with a probability \frac{1}{3} . For n \in \mathbb{N} , a_n , b_n and c_n are the probabilities that, at the end of the n -th year, a consumer will decide to subscribe to A , B or C the following year. a) Determine a recursion relationship between a_n , b_n , c_n and a_{n+1} , b_{n+1} , c_{n+1} . b) Deduce the expression of a_n , b_n and c_n as a function of n . Constant-recursive sequences of order 2 will appear and we will use the following flashcard method . c) Determine the limit of these sequences. Is there an operator which tends towards a monopoly position? Flashcard method: Let (u_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} be a sequence satisfying: \forall n \in \mathbb{N} , u_{n+2} + au_{n+1} + bu_n = 0 , where a, b \in \mathbb{R} are two constants. To find the expression of u_n as a function of n , we use the method of the characteristic equation: i. Consider the characteristic equation X^2 + aX + b = 0 and compute its roots q_1 and q_2 (which might eventually be the same). ii. ★ If q_1 \neq q_2 , we have \forall n \in \mathbb{N} , u_n = \alpha \cdot q_1^n + \beta \cdot q_2^n with \alpha and \beta two constants. ★ If q_1 = q_2 = q , we have \forall n \in \mathbb{N} , u_n = (\alpha \cdot n + \beta) \cdot q^n with \alpha and \beta two constants. iii. The constants \alpha and \beta are found using the data of the problem. More often than not, u_0 and u_1 are known and this yields a linear system of two equations to solve for \alpha and \beta . 3. Discrete Random Variables Often, when dealing with random experiments, we are not really interested in the outcome but rather in a certain quantity related to the outcome. For instance, we can ★ randomly pick a person amongst the french population and measure her height or the average number of sleeping hours per day, ★ randomly pick a third year EFREI student and measure his/her grade in last year's probability final exam, ★ throw two dice and compute the sum of the outcomes. These values that we build out of the outcomes of random experiments are called “random variables” and studying their properties constitutes the heart of probability theory. 3.1 Basic definitions Definition 3.1 (Random variable) Let (\Omega, P) be a probability space. A random variable is simply a function X : \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R} . The set of all possible values of X is called the range of X and is denoted X(\Omega) . The set of all random variables over \Omega is denoted \mathbb{R}^\Omega . Examples: Continuing with the examples of the introduction:

Proposition 3.2 Let X, Y \in \ell(\Omega) be two discrete random variable over \Omega . Then, if the joint probability mass function of X and Y is known, one can deduce the probability mass functions of X and Y (the reverse statement is false!). Proof. Given the joint probability mass function of X and Y , the probability mass function of X is found simply by adding all possible values of Y (and vice-versa): P(X = x) = \sum_{y \in Y(\Omega)} P(X = x, Y = y). (This is, in fact, an application of the total probability formula since the family ((Y = y)_{y \in Y(\Omega)}) is a partition of the sample space.) □

These two random variables are independent. 3.3 Expected Value, Variance, Standard Deviation When working with discrete random variables, we are in fact dealing with a (long) list of pairs of numbers (the x_i and p(X = x_i) ). To describe these lists, it is useful to build some other quantities that capture important characteristics of the random variable. The two most important quantities are the expected value (theoretical mean) and the variance or standard deviation (which measures the dispersion). The expected value corresponds to the theoretical average. For instance, if one has a fair dice with five faces with the symbol "1" and one with the symbol "2", the symbol "2" will, in average, show up once every six throws whereas the symbol "1" will appear five out of six times. Thus, if one throws the dice six times, one can "expect" to have five 1s and one 2. The average result will therefore be \frac{1}{6}(5 \times 1 + 1 \times 2) = 1P(X = 1) + 2P(X = 2) where X denotes the outcome of the throw. In other words, the linear correlation coefficient measures the degree of linearity between X and Y :

• If \rho(X, Y) = 0 , we say that the random variables are not linearly correlated (which does not mean they are independent). • If \rho(X, Y) > 0 , Y tends to increase if X increases. • If \rho(X, Y) < 0 , Y tends to decrease if X increases. • If |\rho(X, Y)| = 1 , Y is a linear function of X .

Example: Let X be a discrete random variable whose support is X(\Omega) = \{-1, 0, 1\} and P(X = -1) = P(X = 0) = P(X = 1) . Moreover, consider the random variable Y = X^2 . The two random variables are clearly dependent but the correlation coefficient will vanish since an increase in X might lead, with equal probability, to an increase or a decrease of Y .

3.5 Probability distributions We will now study in some detail some of the most important probability distributions that one encounters in many situations. 3.5.1 Uniform random variables Definition 3.14 (Uniform distribution) Let X be a discrete random variable. We say that X is uniform if all possible values of X are equally likely. In particular, let n \in \mathbb{N}^* . We denote X \sim \mathcal{U}(\llbracket 1, n \rrbracket) whenever X(\Omega) = \llbracket 1, n \rrbracket \text{ and } \forall k \in \llbracket 1, n \rrbracket, P(X = k) = \frac{1}{n}. Remark: According to the definition, if X is a uniform random variable, X(\Omega) must be a finite set and, for x \in X(\Omega) , we have P(X = x) = \frac{1}{|X(\Omega)|} . Proposition 3.12 : Expected value and variance of a uniform random variable If X \sim \mathcal{U}(\llbracket 1, n \rrbracket) , then E(X) = \frac{n+1}{2} and V(X) = \frac{n^2-1}{12} . Proof. By definition, we have E(X) = \sum_{k=1}^n kP(X = k) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^n k = \frac{n+1}{2}. Similarly, E(X^2) = \sum_{k=1}^n k^2P(X = k) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{k=1}^n k^2 = \frac{(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} and therefore V(X) = E(X^2) - E(X)^2 = \frac{2(n+1)(2n+1)}{12} - \frac{3(n+1)^2}{12} = \frac{(n+1)(n-1)}{12}. □

3.5.2 Bernoulli random variables A “Bernoulli trial” is a random experiment with only two outcomes, called “success” and “failure”. Definition 3.15 (Bernoulli distribution) Let X be a discrete random variable and p \in ]0, 1[ . We say that X is a Bernoulli random variable of parameter p , denoted X \sim \mathcal{B}(p) , if X(\Omega) = \{0, 1\} \text{ and } \begin{cases} P(X = 1) = p \\ P(X = 0) = 1 - p. \end{cases} Examples: There are myriads of examples! ★ Take a person in the French population and check if she is vegetarian ( X = 1 ) or not ( X = 0 ). Then, X \sim \mathcal{B}(0.02) (there is an estimate of 1.4 millions vegetarians in France.) ★ Take a random day in the last ten years and check if it rained in Paris ( X = 1 ) or not ( X = 0 ). Then, X \sim \mathcal{B}(\frac{111}{365}) (in average, Paris has 111 days of rain). ★ Take a second year student at EFREI and check if he or she is a woman X = 1 or not X = 0 . Then X \sim \mathcal{B}(\frac{1}{5}) (there are 20% of woman in L2). Proposition 3.13 : Expected value and variance of a Bernoulli random variable If X \sim \mathcal{B}(p) , then E(X) = p and V(X) = p(1 - p) . Proof. Straightforward computation using the definition. □ 3.5.3 Binomial random variables Let n \in \mathbb{N}^* . Consider n identical and independent runs of a Bernoulli trial of parameter p and denote by X the number of successes. For example, take n atoms of Plutonium ^{240}\text{Pu} and count the number of radioactive decays in an interval of five minutes (each atom behaves independently from the others). Let us find the probability mass function of X . First, there can be from 0 to n successes, therefore X(\Omega) = \llbracket 0, n \rrbracket . Moreover, if X = k , there are n - k failures. Since each run of the experiment is independent from the other ones, the probability of obtaining k successes and n - k failures in a specific order is p^k(1 - p)^{n-k} (follow conditional probabilities along the way in the tree below!). But, be careful!, to compute the probability P(X = k) , one needs to count all the possible paths that lead to k successes and n - k failures: there are as many as there are ways of choosing k objects among n . Definition 3.16 (Binomial distribution) X is a binomial random variable of parameters n and p , denoted X \sim \mathcal{B}(n, p) , if X counts the number of successes in n identical and independent repetitions of a Bernoulli trial where the probability of success is p . In this case, we have X(\Omega) = \llbracket 0, n \rrbracket and \forall k \in \llbracket 0, n \rrbracket , P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k}. Remark: One can check that \sum_{k=0}^n P(X = k) = 1 . Remark: The binomial distribution is associated with successive draws, but it is often considered that, if the size n of the sample to be drawn is small compared with the size of the population N , a simultaneous draw of the sample is equivalent to n successive draws with replacement. We consider the population of France ( N = 67.75 \times 10^6 ), and we are interested in the HIV disease (170 000 people affected). We take a random sample of n = 1000 people (simultaneous draw) and we call X the number of sick people in the sample. Since n/N = 0.000015 is much smaller than 1, we consider that X follows a binomial distribution with parameters n and p = \frac{0.17}{67.75} \approx 0.002 . In other words we treat the simultaneous draw as a successive draw with replacement. Proposition 3.14 : Expected value and variance of a binomial random variable If X \sim \mathcal{B}(n, p) , then E(X) = np and V(X) = np(1 - p) . Proof. There are two methods for the proof: first, use the definition and carry out the computation (this would be a good exercise in the Calculus course SM201). Second, and this is a much more productive approach, viewing X as a sum of independent and identical Bernoulli random variables X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n of parameter p . Therefore, since expected value is a linear map, we have E(X) = E(X_1 + \dots + X_n) = E(X_1) + \dots + E(X_n) = nE(X_1) = np. Similarly, since V(X + Y) = V(X) + V(Y) for independent random variables X, Y V(X) = nV(X_1) = np(1 - p). □ Remark: If we independently fire 200 shots at a target and each time we have a 25% chance of hitting it, we would instantly say that you hit the target 50 times, on average. So, intuitively, and without knowing the formula, we compute np for the expected value. Proposition 3.15 : Sum of independent binomial random variables Let X and Y be two independent discrete random variables such that X \sim \mathcal{B}(n, p) and Y \sim \mathcal{B}(m, p) . Then, we have X + Y \sim \mathcal{B}(n + m, p) . Proof. From the point of view of the previous proof, this result is almost self-evident. Indeed, X is the sum of n independent Bernoulli random variables of parameter p and Y is the sum of m independent Bernoulli random variables of parameter p , therefore X + Y must be the sum of n + m independent Bernoulli random variables of parameter p ! □

Historical Note #2 (The Bernoulli trial and the binomial distribution) The conceptual framework provided by Bernoulli trials and the binomial distribution plays a crucial role in the development of probability theory in the 19th century. It was introduced in 1713 by Jacob Bernoulli in his posthumous work Ars Conjectandi . In particular, therein he proved the first mathematically interesting theorem in probabilities (which he called the “golden theorem”): Bernoulli’s golden theorem Let S_n be the number of successes in n identical runs of a game whose probability of success is p . Then \forall \varepsilon > 0, \lim_{n \rightarrow +\infty} P\left(\left|\frac{S_n}{n} - p\right| < \varepsilon\right) = 1. (In words: the probability of success corresponds, in the long run, to the frequency of successes.) The main mathematical problem in probability theory of the 19th century will be the attempt to clarify and extend this theorem. This will be achieved thanks to the contributions Abraham De Moivre, Pierre-Simon Laplace and Pafnuty Chebyshev. 3.5.4 Negative binomial random variables When dealing with binomial random variables: ★ we fix the number of repetitions of a given Bernoulli trial, ★ we count the number of successes obtained. When dealing with negative binomial random variables, we reverse the situation: ★ we fix the number of successes we wish to obtain, ★ we count the number of repetitions necessary to achieve this.

Definition 3.17 (Negative binomial distribution) X is a negative binomial random variable of parameters r and p , denoted X \sim \mathcal{NB}(r, p) , if X counts the number of independent repetitions of a Bernoulli trial (whose success probability is p ) needed to obtain r > 0 successes. In this case, we have X(\Omega) = \llbracket r, +\infty \llbracket and \forall j \in \llbracket r, +\infty \llbracket , P(X = j) = \binom{j-1}{r-1} p^r (1-p)^{j-r}. ◆ Example: From L3 onwards, an EFREI student who has to take a make-up exam in a certain subject must retake this exam every year until he or she succeeds in passing it. In general, for the L3 mathematics make-up exams, 20% of the exam-takers fail. If we note X the number of times a student has to pass the make-up exam, we have X \sim \mathcal{NB}(1, 0.8) . 2 For instance, you might ask yourself what is the probability that a student will not succeed in validating, before the end of the Master 2, a course that he or she did not validate in L3 (before the make-up exam). We have: \begin{aligned} P(X > 3) &= 1 - P(X = 1) - P(X = 2) - P(X = 3) \\ &= 1 - 0.8 - 0.2 \times 0.8 - 0.2^2 \times 0.8 \\ &\approx 0.008. \end{aligned} Proposition 3.16 : Expected value and variance of a negative binomial random variable If X \sim \mathcal{NB}(r, p) , then E(X) = \frac{r}{p} and V(X) = \frac{r(1-p)}{p^2} . Proof. See exercise 3.22. □ 2 You might expect repetitions not to be independent, but, unfortunately, experience shows that the fact of having already passed the make-up exam has no influence on the result of the next make-up exam ...

3.5.5 Poisson random variables Let us finish with a distribution of a somewhat different nature, mainly associated to rare events , like accidents, radioactive decays, credit default, etc. We will see that in those cases, it is a very good approximation of binomial random variables. Definition 3.18 (Poisson distribution) Let X be a discrete random variable and \lambda \in \mathbb{R}^+ . X is a Poisson random variable of parameter \lambda , denoted X \sim \mathcal{P}(\lambda) , if X(\Omega) = \mathbb{N} and \forall k \in \mathbb{N} , P(X = k) = e^{-\lambda} \frac{\lambda^k}{k!}. The distribution is unimodal and symmetric, centered at k=30. The bars are represented by blue circles connected by thin vertical lines. The peak probability is approximately 0.075 at k=30. Remark: One can check that indeed \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} P(X = k) = e^{-\lambda} \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} \frac{\lambda^k}{k!} = e^{-\lambda} e^{\lambda} = 1. Examples: Here are various examples of variables which can be modelled using Poisson distributions: ★ The number of typos in these lecture notes after proof-reading. ★ The number of patients arriving to a hospital in a given day with a broken bone. ★ The number of people that are 90 years or older in a given community. ★ The number of YouTube videos which surpassed a million views this week. ★ The number of connections to a web server in a given time interval T .

Proposition 3.17 : Expected value and variance of a Poisson random variable If X \sim \mathcal{P}(\lambda) , we have E(X) = V(X) = \lambda . Proof. We have E(X) = \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} kP(X=k) = e^{-\lambda} \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} k \frac{\lambda^k}{k!} = e^{-\lambda} \sum_{k=1}^{+\infty} \frac{\lambda^k}{(k-1)!} = \lambda e^{-\lambda} \sum_{K=0}^{+\infty} \frac{\lambda^K}{K!} = \lambda. Similarly, \begin{aligned} E(X^2) &= \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} k^2 P(X=k) = e^{-\lambda} \sum_{k=1}^{+\infty} k \frac{\lambda^k}{(k-1)!} = \lambda e^{-\lambda} \sum_{K=0}^{+\infty} (K+1) \frac{\lambda^K}{K!} = \lambda \left( E(X) + e^{-\lambda} \sum_{K=0}^{+\infty} \frac{\lambda^K}{K!} \right) \\ &= \lambda^2 + \lambda \end{aligned} and thus V(X) = E(X^2) - E(X) = \lambda . □ The precise reason that explains the importance of Poisson random variables is the following theorem: Theorem 3.18 : Link between binomial and Poisson random variables Let \lambda \in \mathbb{R}^+ . In the limit n \rightarrow +\infty (large number of repetitions), p \rightarrow 0 (successes are rare) and np \rightarrow \lambda (the number of expected successes remains constant), we have \lim_{\substack{n \rightarrow +\infty \\ p \rightarrow 0 \\ np \rightarrow \lambda}} \mathcal{B}(n, p) = \mathcal{P}(\lambda). Proof. Mathematically, the theorem states that \lim_{\substack{n \rightarrow +\infty \\ p \rightarrow 0 \\ np \rightarrow \lambda}} \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k} = e^{-\lambda} \frac{\lambda^k}{k!}. The proof is beyond the scope of this course since it involves Stirling approximation n! \underset{+\infty}{\sim} \sqrt{2\pi n} \left(\frac{n}{e}\right)^n and the limit \lim_{n \rightarrow +\infty} \left(1 - \frac{x}{n}\right)^n = e^{-x}. □

4. Continuous random variables Until now, we have always considered random variables with a finite or countable number of possible values. However, one often encounters the need of using random variables that can take any value in some interval: the lifetime of a radioactive particle, the size of a drop of rain, the distance from the Earth to the nearest galaxy in a given direction, etc. In these situations, the framework changes radically. Mathematically, this is the equivalent of going from sums and series (discrete world) to integrals (continuous world). Conceptually, it is the equivalent of going from atoms to fluids: one has to abandon the notion of probability in a given point (it vanishes) and introduce a “probability density” just as one introduces a charge or mass density in physics. 4.1 Basic definitions Definition 4.1 (Continuous random variables, probability density) A random variable X is (absolutely) continuous if there exists a function f : \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} such that: ★ f \geq 0 ★ \forall B \subset \mathbb{R}, P(X \in B) = \int_B f(x) dx. The function f is called the probability density function associated to the random variable X . The set of all continuous random variables over \Omega is denoted \mathcal{L}(\Omega) .

Methodological flashcard #3 (Probability distribution of Y = g(X) in the continuous case) Let X be a continuous random variable of support X(\Omega) and whose probability density function or cumulative distribution function is known. Let g be a real-valued function defined over X(\Omega) and Y = g(X) a new random variable. To find the probability density function of Y : a) Determine the support Y(\Omega) . b) Express the event \{Y \leq a\} in terms of the random variable X . c) Use this to deduce the cumulative distribution function of Y . d) Differentiate to deduce the probability density function of Y . ◆ Example: Let X be a continuous random variable whose probability density function is f_X(x) = \begin{cases} 1 - |x| & \text{if } -1 \leq x \leq 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} Let us find the probability density function of Y = \sqrt{|X|} . a) First, since X(\Omega) = [-1, 1] , we have Y(\Omega) = [0, 1] . b) Next, let a \in \mathbb{R} . To write the event \{Y \leq a\} , we distinguish three cases: ★ If a < 0 , the event \{Y \leq a\} is impossible. ★ If a > 1 , the event \{Y \leq a\} is certain. ★ If a \in [0, 1] , we have Y \leq a \iff \sqrt{|X|} \leq a \iff |X| \leq a^2 \iff -a^2 \leq X \leq a^2 . c) Therefore, for the cumulative distribution function of Y , we find: ★ If a < 0 , F_Y(a) = P(Y \leq a) = 0 . ★ If a > 0 , F_Y(a) = P(Y \leq a) = 1 . ★ If a \in [0, 1] , \begin{aligned} F_Y(a) &= P(Y \leq a) = P(-a^2 \leq X \leq a^2) \\ &= \int_{-a^2}^{a^2} (1 - |x|) dx \\ &= 2 \int_0^{a^2} (1 - x) dx \\ &= 2a^2 - a^4. \end{aligned} (One can check that F(0) = 0 and F(1) = 1 .)

Definition 4.3 (joint cumulative distribution function) Let X, Y two random variables (discrete or continuous). The joint cumulative distribution function of X and Y is the function F_{X,Y} : \mathbb{R}^2 \rightarrow [0, 1] defined by F_{X,Y}(a, b) = P(X \leq a, Y \leq b). Proposition 4.5 Let X, Y be two random variables (discrete or continuous). Then, if one knows the joint cumulative distribution function F_{X,Y} , one can also know the cumulative distribution functions of X and Y . (The converse statement is wrong!) Proof. Indeed, for a \in \mathbb{R} , we have F_X(a) = P(X \leq a) = P(X \leq a, Y \leq +\infty) = \lim_{b \rightarrow +\infty} F_{X,Y}(a, b). □ Remark: Therefore, all the probabilities about X and Y can be computed from the joint cumulative distribution function. ◆ Example: If one wishes to compute P(X \geq a, Y \geq b) with a, b \in \mathbb{R} , we have \begin{aligned} P(X \geq a, Y \geq b) &= 1 - P(\overline{\{X \geq a\}} \cap \overline{\{Y \geq b\}}) \\ &= 1 - P(\overline{\{X \geq a\}} \cup \{Y \geq b\}) \\ &= 1 - P(\overline{\{X \geq a\}}) - P(\{Y \geq b\}) + P(\overline{\{X \geq a\}} \cap \{Y \geq b\}) \\ &= 1 - P(X < a) - P(Y \geq b) + P(X < a, Y \geq b) \\ &= 1 - F_X(a) - F_Y(b) + F_{X,Y}(a, b). \end{aligned}

The event E = “the child takes back his ball” corresponds to the case where the distance between the ball and the center of the pond is greater than R - r . Therefore, the probability we are looking for is \begin{aligned}

 \end{aligned} Proposition 4.6 Let X and Y two jointly continuous random variables. Then X and Y are both continuous random variables (the converse statement is wrong!). Moreover, the probability density functions of X and Y are given by f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f_{X,Y}(x, y) dy \quad \text{and} \quad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} f_{X,Y}(x, y) dx. The next proposition gives an important property characterising exponential distributions: Proposition 4.12 : Exponential distributions are memory-less We say that a continuous random variable T is memory-less if it satisfies \forall s \geq 0, P(T \geq t + s | T \geq t) = P(T \geq s). Then, we have the following equivalence: T \text{ is memory-less} \iff T \text{ is an exponential random variable.} Proof. See exercise 4.13. □ Remark: We need to understand this property simply: consider, for example, the probability that an electronic component will work for at least s days. This probability is written as P(T \geq s) . The next day, if the component is still working, i.e. "knowing that it has lasted at least one day" ( T \geq 1 ), this first probability will be exactly the same: P(T \geq 1 + s | T \geq 1) = P(T \geq s) . By repeating the reasoning, we realise that, regardless of the number of days that have elapsed, every day the probability that the component will last s days longer will be the same, right up to the moment when it no longer functions. This probability distribution is omnipresent in the modelling of physical phenomena: it is used to describe, for example, the size of the stars in a galaxy, the blood pressure of the human body, the size of a human being and the fundamental state of the quantum harmonic oscillator. Definition 4.11 (Normal or Gaussian distribution) Let X be a continuous random variable and (\mu, \sigma) \in \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^{+*} . X is a normal random variable of parameters \mu and \sigma , denoted X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) , if its probability density function is given by f(x) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}. In particular, if X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1) , X is said to be centered reduced normal distribution .

Methodological flashcard #4 (Computing the probabilities of a normal random variable) Let X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) and I_1, I_2 be two intervals of \mathbb{R} . To P(X \in I_1 | X \in I_2) , one performs the following steps: Introduce Z = \frac{X-\mu}{\sigma} . In this way, Z is a centered reduced normal variable: Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1) . Express the events \{X \in I_1\} and \{X \in I_2\} using the new variable Z . Use the properties of proposition 4.13 to express the probability P(X \in I_1 | X \in I_2) = P(Z \in I_3 | Z \in I_4) in terms of the function \Phi . Use the table of values of \Phi (see next page) to find an estimated value of P(X \in I_1 | X \in I_2) . ◆ Example: Let X \sim \mathcal{N}(6, 4) . Compute P(|X - 4| < 3 | X \geq 2) . Start by introducing Z = \frac{X-6}{2} . Z is a centered reduced normal random variable. Moreover, we have |X - 4| < 3 \iff -3 < X - 4 < 3 \iff -\frac{5}{2} < Z < \frac{1}{2} and also X \geq 2 \iff Z \geq -2. Therefore, we have \begin{aligned} P(|X - 4| < 3 | X \geq 2) &= P\left(-\frac{5}{2} < Z < \frac{1}{2} \mid Z \geq -2\right) \\ &= \frac{P(\{-\frac{5}{2} < Z < \frac{1}{2}\} \cap \{Z \geq -2\})}{P(Z \geq -2)} \\ &= \frac{P(\{-2 \leq Z < \frac{1}{2}\})}{P(Z \geq -2)} \\ &= \frac{\Phi(\frac{1}{2}) - \Phi(-2)}{1 - \Phi(-2)} \\ &= \frac{\Phi(\frac{1}{2}) + \Phi(2) - 1}{\Phi(2)} \end{aligned} Using the table of values of the function \Phi , we find: P(|X - 4| < 3 | X \geq 2) \approx \frac{0.69146 + 0.97725 - 1}{0.97725} \approx 0.68428.

Proposition 4.14 : Expected value and variance of a normal random variable If X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) , then E(X) = \mu and V(X) = \sigma^2 . Proof. Let X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2) . Since Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1) and we have E(Z) = \frac{E(X) - \mu}{\sigma} and V(Z) = \frac{V(X)}{\sigma^2} , it suffices to carry out the computation for Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1) to prove the general case. We have E(Z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{\mathbb{R}} z e^{-z^2/2} dz = 0 since the integrand is an odd function. Similarly, we have \begin{aligned} V(Z) = E(Z^2) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{\mathbb{R}} z^2 e^{-z^2/2} dz \\ &= -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{\mathbb{R}} z \times \left( -z e^{-z^2/2} \right) dz \\ &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{-z^2/2} dz \\ &= P(Z \in \mathbb{R}) = 1 \end{aligned} where, from the second to the third equation, we perform an integration by parts by noticing that -z e^{-z^2/2} is the derivative of e^{-z^2/2} . \square The following theorem, a particular case of the central limit theorem (see the historical note below), largely explains the predominance of the normal distribution in the modelling of physical phenomena: Theorem 4.15 : Link between binomial and normal random variables In the case where n tends to infinity, binomial distributions tends to normal distributions. Let Z_n = \frac{X_n - np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}} the centered reduced random variable associated to X_n . Then, we have \lim_{n \rightarrow +\infty} Z_n \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1).

Historical Note #3 (The normal distribution and the central limit theorem) The normal distribution was first introduced (rather obscurely) by Abraham de Moivre in 1733 to study the limit of binomial distributions. It was Pierre-Simon Laplace who, in his work Théorie analytique des probabilités of 1812, proved an improved version of Bernoulli's golden theorem (see page 76): \forall x \in \mathbb{R}, \lim_{n \rightarrow +\infty} P\left(\frac{S_n - np}{\sqrt{npq}} < x\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^x e^{-y^2/2} dy. This theorem shows that, for big numbers, the discrete Bernoulli trial can be described by a continuous function that will become a key concept in the theory: the normal or Gaussian distribution (thus called because of the use the German mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss made of it). Over half a century later (in 1887), the Russian school lead by Pafnuty Chebyshev succeeds in rigorously stating and proving the central limit theorem , a generalisation of Laplace's result which had been suggested without proof by Laplace himself. This theorem might be the most important result in probability theory: Central limit theorem Let \{X_n\}_{n \in \mathbb{N}} be a sequence of identical and independent random variables of expected value \mu and standard deviation \sigma . Then, \lim_{n \rightarrow +\infty} \frac{X_1 + \dots + X_n}{n} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right). In other words, the normal distribution is a good approximation of the average of any random experiment whatsoever that repeats many times! This is the profound reason behind the omnipresence of the normal distribution.

Exercise 4.21 [***] Study of meteorites (taken from the DE of 2023/2024) A meteoroid is a small body of the solar system whose size ranges between 0.03\text{mm} = 3 \times 10^{-5}\text{m} and 1\text{m} (above this range, we speak of asteroids; below this range, we speak of interplanetary dust). When a meteoroid enters the Earth's atmosphere, it starts to burn and it is then called a meteor or shooting star . When it is big enough to collide with the Earth's surface, it is called a meteorite . We estimate that the average size of a meteoroid is r = 5\text{mm} . Denote by X the random variable that measures the size of a meteoroid. We suppose that the random variable Y = \ln(\frac{X}{r}) follows a normal distribution: Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu = -4, \sigma^2 = (2.83)^2). Compute the probability that X is smaller than 0.1\text{mm} . Knowing that the probability for a meteoroid to become a meteorite is p = 0.002 , find the minimal size a meteoroid must have when entering the Earth's atmosphere in order to be able to hit the Earth's surface. We estimate that tonight there will be n = 1500 shooting stars in the sky (not all visible to the naked eye!). Denote by Z the number of meteoroids that will hit the Earth's surface tonight. Give the probability distribution of Z . Give the expected value E(Z) and its standard deviation \sigma(Z) . Bonus: Prove that indeed, if Y = \ln(\frac{X}{r}) \sim \mathcal{N}(-2.5, (2.24)^2) , then the expected value of X is approximately equal to r . Conclude that, if X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2) and Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2) , then X+Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_1 + \mu_2, \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2) and write the probability density function of aX + bY , for a, b \in \mathbb{R} .

Exercise 4.23 [**] Measuring the Higgs' boson mass The Standard Model of Particles is one of the finest constructions in theoretical physics of the 20th century. In 1964, the British physicist Peter Higgs proposed the existence of a previously unobserved particle that would explain how other particles acquire mass. The mass of a particle is measured in GeV/c^2 , with 1GeV/c^2 = 1.783 \times 10^{-27}kg . In the initial experiment of 2012, they found M_H \sim \mathcal{N}(125.06, 0.0841) . The Standard Model of Particles is one of the finest constructions in theoretical physics of the 20th century. In 1964, the British physicist Peter Higgs proposed the existence of a previously unobserved particle that would explain how other particles acquire mass. This particle was discovered in 2012 by the LHC in Geneva, earning Peter Higgs and François Englert the Nobel Prize.

The mass of a particle is measured in GeV/c^2 , with 1GeV/c^2 = 1.783 \times 10^{-27}kg . In the initial experiment of 2012, they found M_H \sim \mathcal{N}(125.06, 0.0841) . But the experiment had a second run in 2016 and the results gave M_H \sim \mathcal{N}(125.46, 0.0289)^2 .
